clinicalPearls: WWOX encodes a WW-domain-containing oxidoreductase involved in cellular metabolism, apoptosis and neural development; the disorder is autosomal recessive.
The severe end (WOREE syndrome / DEE28) presents with drug-resistant seizures beginning in the first weeks to months of life.
Profound developmental impairment with little or no milestone acquisition and absent visual fixation is typical.
Progressive features include acquired microcephaly, spasticity, dystonia and retinopathy or optic atrophy.
A milder allelic phenotype (SCAR12) causes autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia with epilepsy and intellectual disability.
Genotype strongly influences severity: complete loss of function tends to cause the lethal encephalopathy, whereas hypomorphic variants give milder disease.
Neuroimaging may show a thin corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy and delayed or abnormal myelination.
Seizures are typically multifocal and highly refractory, and premature death in infancy or early childhood is common in the severe form.
reference.pathophysiology: WWOX on chromosome 16q23 encodes WW domain-containing oxidoreductase, a protein with two WW domains and a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase domain that participates in apoptosis, steroid and lipid metabolism, DNA-damage responses and, critically for the nervous system, neuronal differentiation and central myelination. Biallelic loss-of-function or hypomorphic missense variants abolish or reduce WWOX activity, and the genotype-phenotype correlation is strong: null combinations produce the lethal WWOX-related epileptic encephalopathy (WOREE syndrome), while partially functional combinations produce the milder SCAR12 ataxia-epilepsy phenotype. Loss of WWOX disrupts neural metabolic and developmental pathways, resulting in an early developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with progressive atrophy, impaired myelination and refractory seizures.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (STXBP1, KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN2A)
Ohtahara syndrome or early myoclonic encephalopathy of other cause
Neonatal metabolic epilepsies (pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy, non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia)
Congenital cytomegalovirus or other congenital infection
Other autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxias (for the milder phenotype)
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing or a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy gene panel (biallelic WWOX)
EEG (often burst-suppression or multifocal epileptiform activity in the severe form)
MRI brain (atrophy, thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination)
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics (qualitative)
Ophthalmological assessment for retinopathy or optic atrophy
Parental carrier testing and segregation analysis
redFlags: Refractory neonatal or early-infantile seizures with burst-suppression on EEG
Developmental arrest with no visual fixation
Clinical deterioration or apnoeas signalling a life-threatening course
reference.prognosis: The severe WOREE form carries a poor prognosis, with profound disability, refractory epilepsy and frequent death in infancy or early childhood; the milder SCAR12 phenotype is compatible with longer survival but causes progressive ataxia, epilepsy and intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Overlooking a recessive diagnosis in a singleton, particularly with parental consanguinity
Missing the milder allelic ataxia phenotype at the other end of the spectrum
Assuming a structural or acquired cause from imaging atrophy without genetic testing
Failing to offer carrier testing and genetic counselling to the parents
references: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy review literature
management: No treatment corrects the underlying WWOX deficiency, so care centres on seizure control and supportive management of the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
Antiseizure medication for the drug-resistant seizures, typically requiring trials of multiple agents and combinations, with a rescue protocol for prolonged seizures and status epilepticus
Management of spasticity and dystonia with physiotherapy and tone-modifying agents, and prevention of contractures
Nutritional and feeding support including gastrostomy, alongside developmental and palliative input given the profound impairment in the severe WOREE form
Ophthalmological assessment and support for retinopathy or optic atrophy
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology-led care with early discussion of goals of care and prognosis in the lethal phenotype
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with parental carrier testing and segregation analysis
